title: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes”. Scope: native biotas of all countries and regions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Naturalization is well documented globally, but 'perfectly adapted' and 'improved' admit competing fitness definitions. Existing invasion data can test the empirical premise more cleanly than Darwin's broad conclusion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For regional biotas, quantify establishment and impacts of non-native species and ask whether successful invaders outperform natives under shared conditions. The stated inference is supported if every well-surveyed region contains established invaders that displace natives, but invasion without competitive superiority would weaken it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Establishment can reflect human propagule pressure rather than superior adaptation.

The assertion that no native could be improved is not directly entailed by invasion.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Whether non-native species have established in every country is a direct count, and global plant inventories already support it at high coverage. The further inference, that natives were therefore imperfectly adapted and could be improved, is not identified by establishment: several ecological alternatives predict the same lists. A small team could settle the biogeographic pattern quickly and would still lack a clean test of perfect adaptation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each country or flora, count established non-native species and the fraction of the biota they represent. Universal establishment would confirm the naturalisation pattern Darwin treats as evidence; absence of established non-natives from many regions would refute that pattern. Establishment itself would not confirm that native populations could have been improved by selection, because enemy release and disturbance produce the same invasions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Firm possession is a qualitative threshold that checklists do not measure directly.

Invasion success also follows propagule pressure, disturbance, and release from enemies.

Animal naturalizations are less completely tabulated than plants.

fields.label: Dimension scores

data adequacy: 0.74
discriminating power: 0.46
analysis feasibility: 0.82
operationalizability: 0.72
